prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, reaching fractional uncertainties near 10^-18

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B024 for Katori and Ye. The scientific case is a single sharp idea, the magic-wavelength lattice that cancels the light shift of the clock transition so that many atoms can be interrogated at once, followed by a demanding realisation in strontium and ytterbium. Uncertainties near 10^-18 have been reproduced and compared across several countries, and the clocks already deliver centimetre-level relativistic geodesy, tighter limits on drifting constants and a credible route to redefining the second. The discovery is complete, confirmed and attributable to two people. Having read the full round-1 exchange and the chair's questions, I find that the objections to other candidates (unsettled mechanism for B021, credit and 2016 overlap for B030, 2012 overlap for B006) are of at least the same weight as the objections to B024, and none of them has been answered in a way that moves me.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is that precision timekeeping was honoured in 2005 and 2012, so the lattice clock may be read as an increment on a recognised line. I answer the chair's question as follows: the earlier prizes honoured the frequency comb and the control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock solves a different problem, many-atom interrogation without light-shift perturbation, and that is what made the stability and accuracy leap possible. Still, this is a judgment of degree. A two-name prize also passes over Ludlow, Lemonde, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and RIKEN groups who carried the 10^-18 milestone, and the headline payoff, a redefinition of the second or a new-physics limit, has not yet arrived. A committee that weighs discovery of a new state of matter above measurement capability would reasonably rank B021 higher, and the broad appearance of B021 among alternatives is a real signal.

responses.point: Keeps B024 first and, in answer to his own question to the chair, argues that the lattice clock is a distinct invention from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, while conceding that Ludlow, Lemonde and others on the accuracy side are passed over.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of the novelty question and with his insistence that the citation say what is being honoured. I would add that the citation should name the lattice scheme and the 10^-18 result rather than precision measurement in general, so that the accuracy contributors are passed over knowingly and the credit is not mistaken for the whole clock community. I share his concern that the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, but I weigh it less heavily than he does because the capability itself is already demonstrated in several laboratories, whereas the open questions in B021 concern what the observed phenomenon is.

responses.point: Ranks twisted bilayer graphene first for the statistical-physics idea that a twist angle tunes interaction against bandwidth, and concedes that the pairing mechanism is unresolved and that the case is eight years old.
responses.response: I accept the conceptual economy of the twist-angle idea and I do not doubt that the flat-band prediction was correct. His concession on the unresolved mechanism is exactly my reservation. A citation limited to the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated and superconducting phases would be honest, and I would not oppose it if the committee prefers a new platform this year, which is why B021 is my first alternative. But I do not think growth of the literature measures maturity. The clock community has the opposite profile, a narrow question that has been answered and then reproduced.

responses.point: Argues that the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction plus the 2018 observations form a clean theory-plus-experiment pair, and that timeliness favours recognising twisted bilayer graphene now.
responses.response: I agree the pairing of prediction and experiment is clean, and having moved Bistritzer into my reading of the credit I would accept three names. I do not agree that timeliness should decide the matter. Recognising a field while its central open question is unsettled has a cost, and the clock has the same causal chain from idea to measured result without that cost. I would take his point more seriously if the committee were choosing between B021 and B024 as the only two options, and I would then rank B021 above B006 and B030, as my alternatives already show.

responses.point: As chair, supports B030 for Kane, Mele and Molenkamp and, with Danielsson, argues that the 2016 prize did not cover the time-reversal-invariant insulator.
responses.response: I accept that the 2016 prize covered topological phases of matter in a different sense and that the quantum spin Hall prediction and observation are a distinct step. My remaining difficulty is the credit, not the physics. The Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal that Molenkamp's experiment tested and Hasan's three-dimensional work are not captured by the three names, and the citation would have to be written very carefully. I would not oppose B030 if the committee settles the names, but I do not move it above the clock, where no comparable gap exists in the credit among the listed names.

responses.point: Prefers B006 for trapped-ion computation and simulation, arguing it is distinct from the 2012 prize because it concerns gate-based computation, with thirty years of independent confirmation.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction from the 2012 citation and with the confirmation record, which is why B006 remains my second alternative. My hesitation is the experimental credit, since Monroe and the Wineland-lineage work are not named and the Cirac-Zoller gate is no longer the leading gate. That is a manageable problem for a citation on proposal and realisation, but it makes B006 a less clean two-or-three-name prize than B024. I also note the overlap of Cirac and Zoller with B020, which would constrain a later optical-lattice award.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will treat optical lattice clocks as a distinct invention or as an increment on the 2005 and 2012 AMO prizes; this is a judgment about degree that I cannot settle from the files.
Whether a two-name credit adequately identifies the decisive contributors given Ludlow, Lemonde, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and RIKEN groups.
How to weigh a measurement-capability prize against a new-state-of-matter prize this year, and whether B021's broader support should outweigh its unsettled interpretation.
I rely on recalled history, not verified sources, for the order of the clock milestones and for Ye's collaborations.
statement.conflict_note: My profile documents collaborations with Anne L'Huillier and the Lund attosecond group, Ursula Keller's group at ETH Zurich, and Reinhold Schuch, Marcus Dahlstrom, Luca Argenti and Paul Indelicato. None of these people is among the credited names on the shortlisted ballots, so no specific conflict arises. As a theoretical atomic physicist I may lean towards atomic-physics topics, and since my preferred ballot is an AMO candidate I flag that bias again and ask colleagues to weigh my judgment on B024 accordingly.
